I went to Cuba for the salsa, the cigars, the rum and those gorgeous vintage cars. I never imagined that, somewhere between admiring the colourful streets and enjoying the Caribbean sunshine, I would receive an unexpected lesson in money management. Looking back, I can laugh about my experience. But at the time, discovering how much I might have been overpaying left me wondering how much my ignorance had already cost me.

Cuba had a way of making me feel as though I had stepped into a film. Imagine standing in a sun-drenched plaza, a Cuban cigar in your hand, the warm Caribbean breeze brushing against your skin, and music floating through the air. Around you, buildings painted in faded yellows, dusty pinks and weathered blues stand proudly, their grand colonial facades and ornate balconies carrying stories from another century.

Then comes the rumble of an engine. You turn to see a cherry-red vintage car gliding past, followed by a bubblegum-pink beauty that seems to have driven straight out of the 1950s. Everywhere you look, vibrant colours, rich history and lively movement bring the streets to life

And the cars! Oh, the cars!

Later, I would find myself riding in a neon-green convertible along the coast, the wind whipping through my hair as the blue Caribbean Sea stretched beside me. I felt wonderfully alive. Cuba was giving me everything I had hoped for: beauty, music, history and the thrill of discovering somewhere different.

I was so captivated by everything that I paid little attention to the money in my purse.

I visited Cuba in 2019, when the country had two official currencies: the Cuban convertible peso, known as the CUC, and the Cuban peso, known as the CUP. To an unsuspecting tourist like me, this arrangement was a recipe for confusion.

I was carrying CUC notes, commonly used by visitors because that is what the banks give you in exchange for your USD notes. The CUC notes looked different from the CUP notes I would later encounter. CUC notes featured monuments, while CUP notes carried the faces of Cuban national heroes, including José Martí and Camilo Cienfuegos. But at the time, I barely noticed the distinction. Money was money, or so I thought.

Whenever I needed to pay for something, I reached into my purse, brought out my CUC notes and settled the bill. I was enjoying my holiday and had no reason to suspect my wallet was quietly making it more expensive than necessary.

Then, one time, I was given change in a currency different from the familiar CUC. I looked at the notes in my hand and immediately felt that something was wrong. These were not the notes I was accustomed to using. I did not recognise them, and I was not about to walk away with money I did not understand. So, I rejected the change. Imagine my surprise when the cashier and another customer explained to me that the notes were perfectly valid Cuban money! 

That was when I got my crash course in Cuban economics. The country had two official currencies: the Cuban convertible peso (CUC), and the Cuban peso (CUP). I was carrying CUC notes, commonly used by visitors. The notes I had just rejected were CUP notes, used by the locals.

I was relieved, slightly embarrassed and suddenly very curious. How had I been in Cuba for four days without understanding something so fundamental to paying for things?

The top notes (CUC) have monuments and are for tourists. The bottom notes (CUP) have national heroes and are for locals. 

Suddenly, I began wondering how much I had already spent and how I had been paying far more than necessary. I recalled tipping a tour guide 10 CUC. He had been delighted, even asking me whether I was sure I wanted to give him that much. At the time, I thought I was simply being generous. But after learning that the commonly used conversion was around 25 CUP to 1 CUC, I understood why he might have been so pleased. My tip was equivalent to about 250 CUP. I did not regret rewarding someone for good service, but I was beginning to understand how easily a visitor could spend money without appreciating its value.

Then came the experience that really opened my eyes. I had been eating at a particular local food joint and paying 5 CUC for my meal because the menu read $5. I always enjoyed the food and always handed over 5 CUC because 1 USD was equivalent to 1 CUC. But now that I knew about CUP, curiosity got the better of me.

On my next visit, I decided to observe before ordering. A local customer arrived ahead of me. I waited and watched what he ordered, how much he paid and which notes he handed to the cashier.

Five CUP.

Five CUP?

I watched him complete his transaction and leave. Then I stepped forward and ordered the same meal.

When the time came to pay, I brought out my newly acquired CUP notes and handed over 5 CUP. The cashier raised an eyebrow. I pointed to the menu and explained that I had just watched the customer before me order the same meal and pay the same amount. I was not guessing. I got my meal for 5 CUP as against the 5 CUC I had always paid.

At the commonly used conversion rate of 25 CUP to 1 CUC, my previous payment of 5 CUC was equivalent to 125 CUP. I had been paying 125 CUP for a meal that I had just watched a local buy for a mere 5 CUP

Twenty-five times the price!

I was stunned. Part of me wanted to laugh at the absurdity of it all; another part wondered how many other times I had paid without understanding the difference. I had been so confident, so comfortable reaching into my purse and handing over my money. Yet I had missed a detail that could make a significant difference to my spending. That local joint visit became one of my most memorable Cuban experiences. Not because of the food, but because of the lesson I had been taught.

Of course, my story is about Cuba in 2019. The currency system has since changed. On 1 January 2021, Cuba discontinued the CUC as part of a currency reform, leaving the Cuban peso (CUP) as the sole official currency. The two-currency arrangement that caught me off guard belongs to that chapter of the country’s history.

What remains with me, however, is not just the currency confusion. I remember Cuba’s faded pastel buildings, the vintage cars gleaming beneath the sun, the music in the streets and the thrill of driving along the coast in that neon-green convertible. The country was vibrant, beautiful and full of contrasts.

But whenever I travel somewhere new, I remind myself to ask questions, understand the local currency, and never assume I know how things work.

2Baba has announced his upcoming studio album, 'Oldest Young Man', scheduled for release on 27 November 2026. The project marks his first full-length album in six years since 2020's Warriors.

The post “The Legacy Continues”: 2Baba Announces New Album ‘Oldest Young Man’ appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
2Baba wearing a hooded black pleated drape and sunglasses to announce his studio album, Oldest Young Man.

 

Afrobeats icon 2Baba is officially returning with a full-length body of work, and November 27 is the date to mark in your calendars!

The legendary singer and songwriter—formerly known as 2Face Idibia—took to Instagram to announce his upcoming studio album, titled Oldest Young Man.

Taking to social media to share the exciting release date, the Afropop veteran captioned his post:

The legacy continues. OLDEST YOUNG MAN drops 27.11.26. Timeless music, no expiration date.

The announcement marks a huge moment for African music fans. Oldest Young Man is 2Baba’s first studio album in over six years, following his critically acclaimed 2020 project, Warriors, which featured heavyweights like Burna Boy, Wizkid, and Olamide.

While he hasn’t dropped a full-length album since then, the Nigerian music pioneer has remained active with steady releases, most recently dropping singles like “Mental” in September 2026 and “Ifesinachi” earlier in the year.

With over two decades at the top of the game—stretching from his days with Plantashun Boiz to solo anthems like “African Queen“—the legend is set to prove once again why his sound stands the test of time.

Oldest Young Man arrives on all streaming platforms on 27 November 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Funke Akindele, Shoday, and Waje smiling during their London promotional walk ahead of The Four UK premiere.

Upon seeing these photos of Funke Akindele, Shoday and Waje, we had no choice but to pull out our notes, ready for some styling lessons. Did you see how they coordinated their looks for their London outing? Funke and Waje gave us matching buba and iro sets with colourful floral details, while Shoday arrived with a custom embroidered blazer that made its own case for a place in our style notes.

The trio were in the UK for the promotional campaign of The Four: No One Fights Alone, and the outing came with another exciting update. Funke Akindele Network and FilmOne Entertainment have announced that the film will have its UK premiere on 29 November at ODEON Luxe Leicester Square in London, ahead of its worldwide cinema release on 11 December.

Now, if you’re wondering how Funke and Waje managed to wear matching outfits without looking identical, the answer is in the details. Both looks started with off-white textured cotton, but the floral appliqués gave each one a distinct finish. Funke’s outfit features crimson-red roses with spiral stitching across the bodice and bell sleeves, while yellow sunflowers and leafy green stems run down her wrapper. She completed the look with a golden-yellow head wrap, layered gold necklaces, a broad cuff bracelet and metallic red platform sandals.

Funke Akindele Buba and Iro Outfit for The Four London Promo

Waje went for lavender roses across the neckline and sleeves of her blouse, with large green floral appliqués decorating the hem of her wrapper. She kept the colour story going with a matching lavender-trimmed scarf, a gold necklace accented with turquoise stones, coordinating earrings and multi-coloured platform heels. Same base colour, different floral story. We love that.

Waje outdoors in London promoting The Four: No One Fights Alone in a lavender floral buba and iro set.

And Shoday? He clearly had no plans to be the odd one out. His single-breasted blazer featured bold chevron embroidery in turquoise, yellow, red and blue, worn over a beige mesh-knit top and cream wide-leg trousers. Stacked silver Cuban-link chains and dark dress shoes completed the look, giving the colourful jacket room to do its thing.

Shoday in a custom geometric chevron-embroidered blazer during The Four promotional tour in London.

With the fashion notes taken, we’re also looking forward to seeing what the cast has in store for the London premiere. The Four: No One Fights Alone features Funke Akindele, Waje, Chioma Akpotha, Bisola Aiyeola, Richard Mofe-Damijo, Lateef Adedimeji, Timini Egbuson and Uzor Arukwe, among others. The film premieres at ODEON Luxe Leicester Square on 29 November before its global cinema release on 11 December.
